Area of a Circle

AreaLimits
Game: A circle is cut into equal slices and the slices are slid into a long row.
How to play: Change the number of slices and watch the row. What shape does it begin to look like?
6
Look for the math

This is Leonardo da Vinci's picture proof. Nothing is added or taken away: the same pieces are just moved, so the row has exactly the same area as the circle. Make the slices thin enough and the row becomes a rectangle we can measure.

Two wavy edges make one circumference

Each slice has one curved side, an arc of 2πr / N. In the row the slices point up, then down, then up again. Every upward slice puts its arc along the top edge and every downward slice puts its arc along the bottom edge. Together the two edges use all N arcs, so their lengths add to exactly 2πr — one trip around the circumference. With an even number of slices the two edges are equal, each πr. With an odd number one edge has an extra slice, so the row is a curvy trapezoid instead of a parallelogram. The logic test checks this for every count from 3 to 100.

The height becomes the radius

The pointed tips sit in two rows. A slice's sharp point is r · cos(π/N) above the flat rim of its neighbour, and the curved top rises almost a full radius above its own point. The whole row is therefore r(2 − cos(π/N)) tall. As N grows, cos(π/N) approaches 1 and the height approaches r. At 100 slices it is already within one percent — the logic test confirms this for every count.

Where πr² comes from

The row is about πr wide and about r tall, so its area tends to πr · r = πr². That is the area of the original circle, because rearranging pieces never changes their total area. This is a limit: no finite number of slices makes a perfect rectangle, but the more you use, the closer it gets. Try 6 slices, then 12, then 100, and watch the two wavy edges straighten out.

Try 5 slices and then 6. Why does the shape change from a lopsided trapezoid to a balanced parallelogram?
